summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending business. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the appeals and held that the Wealth Tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee interest on the basis of the value of the assets of the assessee ' (i) the assets of which were not confined to cash; (ii) the assets in question, which were not restricted by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assessee; and (iii) the assets which were not covered by any consideration for the assessee ' interest on the securities. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the contentions of the assessee and held that as it maintain the books of account of the assessee, the net wealth on the securities was not liable to be excluded in the wealth Tax assessments of the assesses. The High Court in reference held that the net wealth was liable to include the interest on securities held by the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Wealth tax Officer is not a "net wealth" within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Wealth Tax Act. The WealthTax Officer is not an "net wealth", within the meaning Of section 2(2) of the Act. The expression "net wealth " is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the value of all assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation date". The definition of "net wealth". is defined by el. (m). The expression "assets" is defined by the definition clause (m) to mean "assets, movable or immovable, or both, or both". The definition is defined by section 2(n) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as "the valuation date". Section 2(n), defines "assets", which is a definition clause. The definition is a definition which is not exhaustive of the terms used in the definition. The definition of the expression "assembly of the assessee" is defined in the Income Tax Acts, the Wealth Tax Acts, and the Wealth Tax Rules. The definition in the Wealth Tax is defined by clause (m). "assets " includes "assets". The definition in section 2(g) of the Indian Income Tax Act defines "assembly" as "assets"; the definition is defined in section 2 (n) to mean the assets of every person who is or was a member of a family or a company or a firm or an association of persons or body of individuals whether incorporated or not. The definition includes all the assets of an assessee 's property, whether movable or immovable or not. [310 F H] Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju

The respondent was a Time Keeper in the Beas river Beas river in the State of Punjab. He was incharge of preparing the pay bills and other bills of the work charg ed employees of the project. He made a false identifi tation card in the name of Ashok Kumar Token No. 59 T at serial No. 10 on page 2 of the relevant pay roll. He made this entry with ulterior motive to withdraw the pay of Ashok Kumar for the month of May 1969 even though he was not working in that Division. A bogus identifi ties card in the names of Ashok Kumar, Token No 59 T, was used by him to withdraw the salary of Ashok Kumar. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not a workman within the meaning of the expression "workman" in section 2(s) of the Punjab Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1966. The High court held that the respondent had failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty in as mu ch as he falsely marked the attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar and initiated it under the Punjab Government Servant (Conduct) Rule, 1966, and that the respondent could not be said to be a workman within section 2(k) of the Act. The High 'Court further held that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that it was not a case of misconduct. The High. Court, therefore, allowed the appeal and set aside the order of Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent had ma de his choice of forum and was even otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants ( Conduct) Rules,1966. The Tribunal has to be satisfied that the respondent is not a workman. The respondent has failed to prove that he was not employed in the respondent 's establishment. The respondent having ma de his own choice of forum, and was evenly dealt with und uned government servants, cannot claim that he was a workman within Section 2(k). [36G] 2. The respondent was found guilty of t he charge framed against him. He was found guilty and punished. He was awarded a penalty. The disciplinary authority must, however, be satisfied that he was guilty of t his misconduct. [37H] 3. The respondent, therefore, was found guilty. [38H] 4. The respondent 's misconduct was found to be proved by the Inquiry Officer. The Tribunal was, therefore, right in holding that he was found guilty in the enquiry. [38G]

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for a declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property in question, filed a suit for declaration and an ad interim injunction to restrain him from dispossessing them from the property. The defendants, besides contending that the suit was barred on the principle of res judicata and constructive res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, averred that on the expiry of the lease, the lease stood terminated by efflux of time and defendant No. 2 was, therefore, entitled to let out the property to defendant No. 1 and hence the latter was in lawful possession of the said property. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the suit had been barred on the principles of res judicata. The defendants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the suit filed by the legal representatives was barred on principle of resjudicata and constructive resjudicata as found in the plaint. The High court also found that the plaintiff had paid a sum of Rs. 1200 to defendant No 2 through his employee Dattu Kenkro by way of advance rent for the year ending March, 1968. The Trial court also found the plaintiff had not paid any amount to defendant No 1 as required by the plaintiff. The High 's further finding was that the plaintiff was not in lawful possession and was liable to be evicted. The High. Court also found that there was no evidence on record to show that the plaintiff ever paid any amount towards the rent. The High, therefore, dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit for a decree and an injunction was not maintainable as the suit was not maintainable and deserved to be dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff was entitled to the relief claimed in the suit. [1032C] 1.2 The plaintiff was not entitled to the reliefs claimed in the plaint as the suit had not been filed within the period of limitation prescribed by the Limitation Act. [1033D] 1.3 The provisions of the Limitation Act are not applicable to a suit for possession of a property. The period of limitation for a suit for ejectment of a tenant from the land on or after 1st July, 1962 is a period of three years from the date of the institution of the suit. The period for which the suit is filed is a period during which the suit may be instituted. [1034E] 1.4 The period for the suit is a period when the suit is instituted in a competent court. The period during which a suit is instituted is a period which is of three years. [1035F] 1.5 The period for filing a suit for eviction of a tenant is a period after the commencement of the Act if the suit is not instituted within the period prescribed by the Act. [1045F] 2.1 The period for a suit to recover possession of a building is a period within which the suit can be filed. The period is a period for which a suit can be instituted.

The appellant company was assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fall under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant company was not liable to pay sales tax for the two assessment years. The High Court, however, held that the sales tax was not leviable on the appellant 's goods. The High court, however, took the view that the appellant 'company was not liable for the sales tax for three assessment years 1966 66 and 1967 77 on the basis that they were not liable to sales tax. The High, Court, however held that such was carbons were covered by the entry No. 3 of the Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh Act. The High 'Court also held that the goods under consideration were covered by entry No. 1 of the Schedule and that the appellant was not liable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant is not liable to tax. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The appellant company was liable to pay tax for the first assessment years 1967 66 and 1968 77 on the goods under assessment. [561E] The appellant company is liable to pay the sales tax on the goods manufactured by it. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon is used. [562F] The appellant 's case that the goods were manufactured by the appellant company were not correctly classified under entry No 4 of the Schedule. The appellant company had not produced the original or printed material before the Sales Tax Appellate Authority. The High. Court was right in holding that such is carbons are covered by the entries in the Schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. [563F G] The appellant is liable to be taxed. The High Courts rightly held that the main use of the are carbons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact of production of promotional measures like telephone, etc., is not conclusive. [564G H] The appellant Company is liable to tax for the entire assessment year 1965 66. The appellant 'company is liable to sales Tax for the first year 1965 67. The appellant is not entitled to the benefit of the exemption under the notification. [565G] The appellant was liable to be assessed to sales Tax on the goods covered by the relevant entry No. 2 for the assessment year 1966 77. The appellant was not entitled to claim the benefit of exemption under the Notification. [566A] The appellant has not produced the copy of the original or the printed material before it. The appellant has produced the original and printed material before this Court. The appellant Company was not liable in respect of sales tax for these two assessment years,

The petitioners challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the (67 of 1957) amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the notification was ultra vires the State Legislature and that the notification issued by it was ultra vires. The petitioners also contended that the State Government had no power to issue a notification under section 15 of 1957 and that the State was not bound to issue the notification under section 9 of the Act. The State Government contended that the power to issue the said notification was not delegated to the State Government and that the power was not delegated. The State of Gujarat, on the other hand, contended that the impugned notification was ultra virus and that the impugned notifications were ultra vires the provisions of the Act and that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the notification. The State contended that the Act was ultra vires and that the Act did not violate article 301 of the Constitution. The petitioners further contended that the provisions of section 9 of Gujarat Minor Mineral Concession Rules 1966 were ultra vires and the State Government was not bound by the provisions of that Act. The petitioners submitted that the impugned Notification was ultra vires as it was not a law made by the State Legislature. The petitioners, therefore, prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to issue a mandamus to the State to issue a Notification under section 15(1) of the Act amending the Gujarat Mineral Rules 1965. The State Legislature passed the Gujarat Minor Minerals Rules 1966 which was published in the Gazette on June 26. The petitioners challenged the vires of the Act on the ground that the Act had been enacted with a view to provide for the regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was not open to the State Legislature to issue the same. The petitioners urged that the impugned Act was ultra viro the Constitution and that the provisions in the Act were ultra vires. Dismissing the petitions, the Court, HELD: 1. The impugned Act is ultra vires the Constitution. [416D] 1. The Act is not a law enacted by the Parliament and the State Legislature is competent to enact it. The Act has made provision with regard to the issue of prospecting licences and mining leases in respect of various kinds of minerals other than minor minerals and the procedure to be followed in the matter of issue of prospecting licence and mining leases. [416E] 2. The impugned notification was not ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 246 of the Constitution and the State Act was not ultra virus. [416F] 3. The impugned notifications were not ultra vires. [416G] 4. The impugned Notification was not ultra law. The State legislature was competent to enact the impugned Act. The impugned Notifications were ultra vires as they were not made under the provisions of any law. [416H] 5. The impugned provisions of the impugned notifications are ultra vires the power of the State legislature. The impugned orders are ultra vires. They are not ultra vires of the Constitution, and are therefore, liable to be quashed. [416C]

The position that the appellant held a hereditary office was that of a hereditary office, and the office that was held by him was not hereditary at all.

The appellant was the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff, who died on July 7, 1949. After the death of Amarchand N, the arrangement between the two partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of the work done up to the death of the old and the old and new and the old, the realisations were to be divided amongst the old and old and the new and the new. and the old were to be assessed to income tax under section 24B of the Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer assessed the amounts in the hands of the heirs and the legal representatives of Amarchand as a Hindu undivided family. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment on the ground that the amounts were not the income of the Hindu undivided family but were not liable to be taxed in the hands and that the income tax authorities were not competent to assess the income in the hands. The High Court held that the amounts could not be taxed in respect of income which were not received in the previous year and were therefore not liable to tax. The appellant contended that the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which were not the assessee were not liable. Held, that the amounts sought to be assessed were not the Income tax Officer, but the Income tax officer was entitled to assess the total income of the deceased person as if the legal representatives were the assessees and the amount was liable to tax under section 23(4) of the Income Tax Act. The income tax authorities could not be said to be liable to tax in respect of that year. The income of the assessee was not liable to the tax. The income was not liable for the assessment year in respect of which the income was assessed. The income which was liable to be assessed was not liable. The income could not be assessed to tax in the hands or the heirs and, legal representatives who could be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years. The income in the present case was not liable, but the income tax officer was not entitled to assess it. The income received by the deceased was not liable as income which was not liable under section 24 B of the Income. tax Act.

The appellant was a trade union officer. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and in two of the three appeals, he was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant was convicted and convicted under section 52. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was restricted to the acquittal of the appellant in respect of offences under section 411 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three cases. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 411 of Indian Penal Code, as the appellant had not been convicted under section 411. Held, that the appellant could not be convicted under section 414 of the Indian Evidence Act, because, he had the opportunity to obtain the articles seized from the house in which the articles were seized. The appellant had the opportunity of obtaining the articles from the post office and had the opportunity, to get the articles seized, to be in the possession of the appellant. The appellant could not, therefore, be convicted under the section. The appellant must be deemed to be in exclusive possession of the articles seized. The fact that the articles were found in the almirah was not a circumstance which would justify the inference that the almirah were in the possession and possession of the respondent. The appellant, therefore, could not be held guilty under section 411 Of the Indian Penal code. The appellant has not been convicted for the offence under section 411 but has been convicted for an offence under section 414. The appellant is entitled to the protection of section 411 Of Indian Penal Code and the appellant must be held to be in possession of the almirah in the manner prescribed by section 411 Of that Code. The appellant cannot be convicted under that section. The fact of the almirahs being in the possession or possession of the person who was in possession of a almirah which was in his exclusive possession does not make the prosecution case against the appellant.

(iii) The High court was right in taking the view that the High Courts had no jurisdiction under section 85(1) of the Act to stay further proceeding before the Nysya Panchayat. [117 C] (iv) The High ' Court was right when it held that the orders of the Nyshadd Court were not vitiated by the fact that the reasons for not accepting the mere statement of the party that the HighCourt had stayed proceedings before them. The appellant Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the State of Madhya Pradesh, issued a public notice under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963, to the respondents to show cause why the names of the respondents be not included in the electoral roll of the Municipal Corporation of Bilaspur. The Full Bench of the High Court held that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body meeting, it was not possible to calculate the period of 30 days specified in that section and it would not be possible to give effect to the provisions of section 220 and, therefore, the balance sheet and profit and loss account were not laid before a special body meeting. The Full bench, however, held that if the balance sheet was not laid before the general body meeting and the balance sheet of profit and loss accounts were not laid, the balance sheets and profit and losses account were not available for inspection and the balance sheets were not available. The Full Court also held that if there was a balance sheet and loss account, the balancesheet and profit and Loss account were not placed before the general meeting, the balance Sheet and profit and the profit and loss Account were not laid. The Full court also held that the balance sheet, profit and loss and loss account had not been laid before a particular meeting and that the balance sheets, profit and losses and profit and profit and, loss account were also not available for the purpose of the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Full Bench was right in holding that the balance Sheet, profit and Loss Account were not available to the appellants. The Full Benches of the High Courts had held that the provisions of sections 32 and 131 of the , were not attracted to the case. [414 F] (2) The Full Court was right in rejecting the contention that the balancesheet, profit and profit account and profit and profits account were not provided for in the balance sheet. The Full view of the Full Bench was correct. [414 G] (3) The Full bench was right in observing that the Full Bench had not laid down any general principle that the balance-sheet and profit & loss account should be laid before a specific body meeting. [414 H] (4) The Full Benches had held that section 25 of the Act was not applicable to the case and that the section in the English Act was a composite one and that the provisions in section 25 of that Act were not applicable to it. [414 C] (5) The Full view that the balanceheet and profit and Profit and Loss Account are not available to a prosecution under section 134 of the Act is not correct. The Full majority view of the High court was correct. The majority view of this Court in The State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors. , relied on.

The respondent was convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment by the Special Court established under section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 (2) of the Act was ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court held that the Special court had no jurisdiction under article 226 to try the respondent and the High Court had no power to issue a writ of mandamus to quash the conviction and the sentence. Held, that the Special Courts had no jurisdiction in the matter and the High Courts had no power under article 226 in the matter of granting a writ of writ of certiorari to quash the sentence. The power of the High Court to issue a Writ of certiorari to issue a mandamus to quash a conviction and sentence is not confined to the power of the Court to issue such a writ. The power to issue writs of certiorari is not confined only to the power to issue such writs and the power to quash the same is not confined merely to the power conferred by the Constitution. It is not necessary for the purpose of this case to go into the question whether the power of issuing writs of certiorari to the High Courts is confined only to cases where the exercise of the power is not in accordance with the Constitution. Held, further, that the power of issue of writs of certiorari under article 226 is not confined in its scope to the power exercisable by the High Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction under article 32. The power is not confined within the scope of the power conferred on the High Court by article 226. The power conferred on High Court by the Constitution is not confined exclusively to the power exercised by the High Courts in the exercise thereof. The power under article 32 is not confined either to the power or the power conferred under the Constitution. In the exercise of that power the High Court is not bound to issue a writs of certiorari. The power given to the High court under article 226 cannot be exercised in the exercise by the High court of its jurisdiction to issue a prerogative writ of certiorari.

The Tribunal held that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was no identical industry in the region in which minimum wage was higher than the minimum wage paid by the company, but failed to fix the minimum wages in the award in accordance with the minimum wages being paid in those industries. The Tribunal, however, held that the award of the Tribunal was not applicable to the case. The Tribunal accordingly held that the tribunal had no jurisdiction. The appellant appealed to this Court. The assessee, a partnership firm, filed a return of income for the assessment year 1960 61, under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961, for the assessment years 1960 61 and 1961 61. The Income tax Officer, Ward A, held that the assessee was liable to pay income tax for the assessment for the year 1960 62, and that the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to issue a notice under section 148. The Income Tax Officer, Ward B, held that there was no reason to believe that the assessee had concealed the income chargeable to tax for the year in question. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that no notice under section 147 was necessary. The Appellate Tribunal, however, dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Income tax Act is a self contained code in respect of income chargeable to income tax. The Income. tax Officer has to be satisfied that it is a fit case for the issue of a notice under Section 148. He has to be either of the opinion that it is not a fit case to issue notice under section148. [455 B C] (ii) The Commissioner has to be of the opinion on the material before him that the assessee has concealed the income of the chargeable to tax. (b) of section 147. Therefore he could not have issued a notice under s. 148. [458 D]

The petitioner, Suraj Mall Mohta and Co. Ltd., is a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1953. The petitioner, a company registered in the Indian Companies, was registered under the Income tax Act, 1922. The Central Government referred these cases to the Investigation Commission under the provisions of section 5(4) of the Act and the cases were numbered 831/64 in the records of the Commission. The petitioner was a managing director of another company, Messrs Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. A reference was made by the Central Government under section 5(1) of the , to the Investigation Commis sioner, who was the managing director of the other company, and the petitioner was the managing Director of another company. The petitioner challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act on the ground that the provisions of sections 5(1), 5(4), 6 and 7 of the Act had become void as discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the Constitution of India. The petitioner contended that the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in sections 6 and 7 was not fair and that the procedure for assessment and recovery of tax was adequate to prevent evasion of tax and that the provisions in sections 5(4, 6 and 7 were not saved by the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the procedure under section 5 of the Act was substantially prejudicial to the assessee and the procedure prescribed in section 5(2) of the impugned Act was not violative of article 14. The procedure prescribed in sections 6, 7 and 8 of the Act in sections 5, 6 and7 of the Act, in so far as affects the persons proceeded against under that section being a piece of discriminatory legislation, infringed the fundamental rights of the petitioner. The procedure for assessment of tax was not adequate to prevent the evasion of tax. The procedure under section 6 and 7, in so much as the procedure prescribed under section 5 were not adequate to enable the Income tax Officer to assess the tax and recover the tax, were reasonable and the procedure for recovery of tax had to be followed. The procedure in section 5 was not a fair and reasonable procedure and the procedure in section 6 was not a proper and fair procedure. The procedure followed in sections 6 to 7 was not a just and reasonable procedure. The provisions of section 6 and the procedure under sections 5(2), 6 and7 were not violative of the provisions. The procedure of section 5 was a reasonable and fair procedure and the provisions of that section were not violative. The procedure adopted in sections 6 & 7 was not in accordance with the procedure prescribed for the assessment and recovery. The procedure provided in section 5 of Act XXX of 1947 was not a reasonable and proper procedure and the procedures prescribed by the Act in section 5 were therefore not violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and were therefore void.

The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi, was registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The primary object of the Federation was to promote Indian business in matters of the trade and business of the Federation. The Federation was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The Federation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Federation 's order dated February 8, 1967, and the High Court held that the Federation was a 'commercial establishment ' within the meaning Of section 2(7) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The High Court held the Federation was not a "commercial establishments" within the definition of "commercial establishment". The Federation appealed to this Court. HELD: The Federation was not an "commercial establishment", within the meaning ofs.2(5) Of the Act. [357 B] The Federation was an "commercial organisation" within the Act. It was not a 'commercial activity ' because by the Memorandum of Association, the Federation was established for a "commercial purpose" within the ambit of section 2 (5) of Delhi Shops and Establishment Act, 1956. The Federation had no business or trade in its business. The Federation could not, therefore, be a "commercial activity" within the purview of section 2 of the Act, and the Federation could not be a "industrial establishment" within section 2(27) of the Indian Act. [359 C D] The Federation had a secretary, and the members of the Federation were not members of the association. The Federation did not carry on any business carried on by the Federation. [358 C] The Federation could be a "Commercial establishment" within its meaning of section2(5). The Federation could only be a "business" within the scope of section 2. (5) Of Delhi Shops and establishments Act, 1957. The Federation cannot be a " commercial establishment" within Section 2(27). The Federation cannot, therefore, fall within the definition 'commercial establishment ', because by the memorandum of Association, it was established for the objects of preparing and publishing under gratuitous professional control, reports of judicial decisions, of issuing digests and other publications relating to legal subjects. [352 C D] R. K. Mittals case, (supra) referred to.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family consisting of a descendant of one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh who was then the original founder of the estate. The appellant was the original owner of the estate and the estate was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant claimed that the grant of the grant to the Raja Chet Singh was not a revenue receipt but a revenue receipt. The Income tax Officer held that it was not a capital receipt but a capital receipt. The High Court in reference held that the grant was not a tax on income. The High court in reference held in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The grant was not in the nature of a revenue receipt and was not a payment of the compensation for relinquishing the title to those lands. The grant was in the nature taxable. The grant did not fall within the definition of a revenue expenditure. [707 E] The grant was a revenue receipt, and the payment was in the character of revenue receipt. [709 E] The payment was in fact a payment of compensation for relinquishes the title to the lands in dispute. The payment was not a receipt of revenue. The grant could not be regarded as a revenue receipt because the grant was in fact an annuity. The grant, therefore, did not fall under the definition of revenue expenditure. The grant fell within the definition. [706 E] The amount of revenue income was not taxable. The amount of the grant was therefore not a revenue expenditure and the grant was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipts. [704 E] The High Court was right in holding that the grant fell within section 4(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1924. [705 E]

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charged with criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51, and the prosecution was that he had misappropriated the amount of his wages to the workmen employed in the works, and the procedure usually followed was that he was to receive the amount from the treasury, and paid the same to the emplo yees against their signatures or thumb impressions. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 465 and section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years and a fine of Rs. 1,000. The High Court, on appeal, held that the prosecution was not barred by section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and that the conviction was illegal. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was illegal. The conviction was illegal for want of sanction, but the conviction was not illegal. The appellant was not charged with criminal breach of trust. The conviction of the accused was illegal for the prosecution of the appellant on the charge of criminal misappropriation. The conviction could not be sustained under section 465 of the Indian Evidence Act. The conviction under section 465 was illegal for failure to comply with the provisions of section 197(i) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The conviction is illegal for wantof sanction, but it is not illegal for want on the part of the appellant to prosecute the case. The conviction cannot be sustained under the section because the conviction was one under section 465. The conviction must be set aside. The conviction can be set aside on the ground that the offence charged is committed in the course of the service of the Government or a public servant. The appellant could not be convicted under section 465 because he was not charged under section 465 but under section 409 of Indian Penal Code. The appellant had not been charged with criminal conspiracy to commit criminal misappropriation of the Government money entrusted to his care as a public servant, and the conviction was therefore illegal. The appeal must be allowed. The conviction and sentence of the appellant must be setaside. The conviction should be quashed.

The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Tribunal was unsuccessful but the Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax, it was entitled to deduction of the losses incurred in the previous year in the previous years. The High Court in reference, held that the company had no business loss in the previous accounting year and that the loss of the company could not be deducted from its profits. Held, that the company being a public limited limited company, the profits of which were exempted from payment of tax in British India were not liable to be deducted from profits of the previous year. The business in the present case was to be assessed to income of the previous years and not to the income of a company. The business was one and indivisible and the profits of a company were exempt from tax in British territory. The business could not be said to be one and indivisible, for the purpose was to be taxed in British India. The business which was to be taken into account was to be the business of a company in which the company was carrying on the business and the profits were to be deducted therefrom. The business carried on by the company was one and the same as it was carrying on its business.

The Tribunal must have regard to the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on the record. The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine. Held, that the presumption was not drawn by the prosecution and the appellants were rightly convicted under section 396. The presumption under section 113 of the Indian Railways Act was not rebutted by the appellants. The presumption was not rebutted. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is. committed. The reason is obvious. Disposal of the fruits, of crime requires the finding of a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determined whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. The presumption may be reduced to the extent that the person who has the goods in possession received them is the dacoits themselves. The presumption, therefore, must be drawn in the case of a person with whom the goods were found. The presumption can be drawn only in the case where the person with whom a person is found is the dacoit or the person who is in possession of the goods. The presumption of the person with whose goods are found is not rebutted. In the present case the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the stolen goods were found in their houses. The houses were found to be in the possession of the appellants and the appellants. In some of the cases there may also be other elements, the appellants might have disposed of the property to these appellants or the dacoits. The presumption in this case was not drawn in the present case.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1950, on the ground that he was in the Indian Air Force as an emergency Commissioned Officer, and was therefore, not furnished with the particulars of the grounds of detention. The grounds of detention were vague. The grounds were vague. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the grounds of the detention were vague and that the grounds were vague and the grounds were not vague. Held, that the grounds did not constitute the grounds of preventive detention. The fact that the grounds related to the decision of the detaining authority itself, taken at the time of making the order of detention, did not make the order of preventive detention illegal. The grounds did not contain any particulars of the ground of detention. It was not necessary to disclose the facts in the grounds of grounds of detention to be vague. The order of detention was not mala fide. The fact of the grounds did no affect the constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in the circumstances of the case. The requirement of the grounds was not a mere formality. The requirement was not a condition precedent to the exercise of the power. The requirement to disclose facts considered against public interest was not a requirement of the statute. The requirement that the grounds should be vague must be communicated to the detenue at the time when the grounds were furnished. The requirement must be clearly communicated to the detenu at the time the grounds were supplied. The requirement is not a condition of the statute and the requirement must be communicated. The requirement may be express or implied in a situation where no particulars are at all furnished. The obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts, and the nature of the grounds on which the detention is based, are not a condition for the exercise of a power. The obligation is not a requirement to communicate the grounds to the detenue. The obligation must be express or in the nature of a condition. The obligation cannot be implied as a condition of a valid order. The obligation can be implied in a condition of an order. The requirement can be waived by the detaining authority. The obligation may be express in a situation which is not contemplated by the statute. In the present case there was no merit in the contention that the grounds could be furnished in public interest. The requirement in the grounds was vague and the non disclosure made in the affidavit of the Under Secretary was not a sufficient compliance with the requirements of article 22(5) to enable the detaining authority to make a proper representation. The requirement could not be waived by a mere formality or a condition of being supplied. The obligation was not a compliance with the requirement of the law. The obligation of the detaining Authority to communicate the reasons for its decision was not a mandatory requirement. The obligation under article 22(6) of the Constitution cannot be implied. The obligation on the detenue to give particulars of the reasons for the detention was not a substantive obligation. The obligation in the present case was not a provision of law and the requirement was not an obligation to inform the detenue at all. The obligation, therefore, could not be implied in this case.

The appellant, a registered partnership firm, applied to the District Magistrate, Jammu under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 for permission to construct a new cinema hall. The District Magistrate, by his order dated July 22, 1966, directed the suspension of the cinema hall. On July 22,1966, the District Magistrate issued a notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be suspended. The appellant challenged the order of suspension by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The power to suspend a licence is conferred only by section 6 F of the Act, as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the section are present, the licensing authority had no jurisdiction to suspend the licence. The power of suspension of licence is conferred by section 6 of the Act. The power is conferred only under section 6 F and not under section 6. The power conferred on the District Magistrate under section 6 is not a power to suspend the cinema hall and the power to administer and enforce the provisions of that section is not a matter of mere formality. [594 C D] 3. The power under section 6 of Jammu and the Act is a special one. The power can be exercised only by the District Magistrates under section 6 and not by the District magistrate. The power has been conferred only by Section 6 F of Jammu and Jammu and Kashmir Act. The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants and the appellants were put in possession of the mills and the factory. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari to quash the notice and the writ of certiorari issued by the High Court. The appellants contended that the respondent had no authority to sell the mills and that the respondent was not entitled to cancel the lease in their favour, and that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of the Act. Held, that the respondent could not be said to have been acting within his authority in issuing the notice under section 12 of the Act, and that it was not necessary for the respondent to have issued the notice in question under section 12. The section expressly authorised the custodian to cancel the notice and to make a fresh notice. The section was intended to be retrospective in operation and it was not intended to affect the rights of the appellants in the matter of the lease. The section did not confer any authority on the custodian to cancellation the lease in favour of the appellants. The section merely authorised the custodian, to cancel the agreement, and the respondent could be said to be acting within his powers in issuing the lease. It was not necessary to make a reference to the section. The section clearly intended to repel a possible contention that section 12 did not by implication repeal statutes confer rights on lessees, and cannot be reconciled with the contention of the appellants that it conferred no authority on him to cancel the contract. The section further stated that the power to cancel a lease may be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The section expressly authorises the custodian to vary the terms of the lease, and the section does not confer any power on the custodian or the Custodian to cancel the same. The section does not authorise the custodian to revoke the lease in his favour. The section only provides that the custodian may cancel the lease if he is satisfied that the lease is not in accordance with the terms of a lease. The respondent was acting within his power in issuing the notices under section 12 and the appellants had no authority under section 12 to cancel the said lease in their absence. The section also does not authorise any such authority to cancel the order of the Custodian. The section, therefore, did not authorise the Custodian to revoke the notice in his favour, and the appellants could not be asked to cancel the notices.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of land in favour of the appellants in the year 1949 and the appellants were allotted lands in the same village. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General, Evacuee Property, but the Additional Custodian for the State of Punjab cancelled the allotment of the lands in favour of them. The Additional Custodian, however, dismissed the revision application on the ground that the allotment was made in favour of a displaced person. The Additional Director of Evacuee Property, however, rejected the revision application and the Custodian General confirmed the order of the Custodian. The appellants preferred an appeal to the Custodian General. The Custodian General, however, allowed the appeal and the Custodian was directed to restore the land to the appellants. The appellants moved the Custodian General for a review of the order of cancellation of the allotment. The Custodian, however dismissed the application on the view that the order of allotment was not a transfer of property but was a transfer of the property to the Custodian. On appeal the Custodian General held that the order was a transfer and that the order cancelling the allotment was a transfer. The Custodian appealed to the Custodian and the Custodian appealed to this Court. Held, that the order passed by the Custodian was a transfer within the meaning of section 12 of the Evacuee Property Act and was not a sale within the meaning ofs.10 of the Act. The order of cancellation was a transfer in the sense that it was a transfer by way of transfer. The order was a sale in the sense of a transfer by the transferor to the transferee. The transfer was a transfer to the transferee and the transfer was a sale. The transfer in the present case was a transfer made by the transferor and the transferee was a transfer from the transferee to the transferee, and the transfer in the instant case was a sale within section 12 of that Act. The transfer of the land in favour was a transfer for a consideration which was not a mortgage or a transfer for consideration. The transfer could not be said to be a transfer of land within the meaning Of section 10 of the Act and was therefore a transfer within section 12. The order passed by him was a transfer which was a transfer under section 12 of Act and was a transfer without any transfer. The transfer, therefore, was a transfer not a transfer but a transfer of a property. The order did not amount to transfer of property within the meaning and scope of section 10 of Act. The Custodian was not entitled to make a transfer of any property. The Custodian could not, therefore, be permitted to make a new transfer of the lands. The order cancelling the allotments was a transfer, and the order was not a cancellation of the allotments. The order could not be made a transfer of an immovable property within the definition of section 10. The order, therefore, did not amount a transfer within s.10 of Act.

They purchased certain raw materials in the State without paying tax thereon in view of the provision of section 24 of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. They purchased raw materials in State without paying the tax thereon in spite of the provision in section 24 of that Act. They then manufactured certain goods in the State with the aid of the said raw materials. They then sold the manufactured goods to dealers who in turn sold those goods out of India. On these facts, it was claimed, that the assessees were not liable to pay the purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Act. The assessees contended that the purchase tax was not leviable on the raw material imported by them. The assessees, therefore, contended that the purchases were not liable for the purchase tax. The assessees also contended that the assessees had purchased raw materials from the State without payment of tax and that the assessees could not be held liable for the purchases tax on the purchase of raw materials. The assessees disputed the correctness of the stand taken by the assessees. The taxing authorities rejected the contentions. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessees that the purchase of the raw materials by the assessees was not liable to be taxed as a sale in the hands of the assessees. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The purchase tax on raw materials is not leviable on a sale in a State in the hands or the dealer who purchases them. The only exception is the limited class of goods covered by section 9 but even this exception has been left out with complete retro spective effect. [347C D] 2. The purchase of raw material is not liable to tax under section 9 but under section 24(1) and the purchase tax is leviable on the purchase price of the raw material. [347E] 3. The purchase price of raw materials is the price at which the raw materials are purchased and the purchase price is the price which is the price of the goods. The purchase value of the rawmaterial purchased by the assessees is the price that is the price. The purchase is not liable for tax under section 6. [347F] 4. The purchase turnover of the raw raw materials is taxable under section 5(3) of the C.S.T. Act, 1956 and the same transaction cannot be taxed as sale in the course of export out of the territory of India within the meaning of section 5(1) or section 24(2) of the Central Sales Tax Act. The purchase in the instant case was not liable for purchase tax. [347D] 7. The purchase was not liable.
